newsitem.title: PERU: Peru seeks to restart talks with Marxist captors.
newsitem.headline: Peru seeks to restart talks with Marxist captors.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori's government sought on Wednesday to restart stalled talks with Marxist rebels who have held 72 hostages inside the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima for 50 days.
Police checked security at a house near the residence selected for a possible meeting between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini.
Fujimori also said he was organising "a meeting on logistics ... and a meeting between minister Palermo and the (four) guarantor members" nominated to observe talks.
"We then hope to define the sequence of these preliminary conversations (with the MRTA)," he added in comments to reporters during a tour of a Lima shantytown.

There was no evidence, however, that the main obstacle to a direct meeting -- the government's refusal to consider the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) demand to release some 400 jailed comrades -- was even close to being removed.
Soon after dawn, the roughly 15 MRTA fighters in the residence defiantly broadcast their revolutionary anthem in honour of dead comrades and pledged not to abandon their goal.
"What is the objective of this mission?" Cerpa shouted through a megaphone. "Liberty for the prisoners," his fellow MRTA members replied.
Returning to Peru after a five-day foreign tour, Fujimori said on Tuesday night he would "look at every imaginative way possible" to free the captives.

Fujimori, whose younger brother Pedro is among the hostages, promised Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto at a weekend summit in Toronto he would resume negotiations with the MRTA. There have been no direct talks between the two sides since Dec. 28.

But while the government expressed its desire to talk, it maintained a heavy police presence outside the residence and sent a military plane roaring over the residence in the early afternoon at a height of about 1,000 feet (300 metres).

The MRTA rebels were demanding the release of jailed comrades in return for a array of hostages that included two government ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors and nearly two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.

Fujimori, who built a reputation for being tough on Peru's guerrilla movements, rejected this demand but has floated the possibility of easing harsh prison conditions and allowing the hostage-takers to seek asylum abroad.

His brief stopover on Tuesday in the Dominican Republic, where he met President Leonel Fernandez, fuelled speculation the Caribbean nation could provide refuge for the MRTA. Cuba, from whose revolution the MRTA draws its inspiration, also has figured in the rumours swirling round Lima.

Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, one of the four "guarantors" who has frequently entered the residence to converse with Cerpa and check on the state of the hostages, urged both sides to tone down their militant public stances.

"It would help to improve the language, improve the attitude, and thus manage to quickly advance the start of conversations," he told local radio. He also urged an "inner change in the positions of both parties," in apparent allusion to the stalemate over the MRTA prisoners.

A survey released on Wednesday by pollster Datum said 40.8 percent of Peruvians believed the government's biggest success so far in the crisis had been to reject the MRTA's demands. Another 15 percent said the government had had no success, while 13 percent said protecting the hostages' lives was the main achievement.

The poll of 400 residents in the capital also showed that 28 percent thought the government's biggest error prior to the crisis was to neglect security at the diplomatic residence, while 17.8 percent said it was the failure to strengthen the overall fight against terrorism in Peru.
